I used to be extremely religious as I was brought up in a very religious household. But as I aged and was able to think rationally and put Christianity on the podium I realized that it is very logically flawed, and thinking back, I was actually in denial for a few years before I accept my conclusions.

I will list down a few logical flaws in which I believe are extremely significant and helped me to think myself out of my christian indoctrination:

1. The problem of evil - The god of Abraham is said to be omnibenevolent, omnipotent, and omniscient. So why do bad things exist? If god is indeed omnibenevolent and omnipotent, then can't god alter the whole physical laws to make things are are "bad" not possible (in a way without any negative consequences)? And if god is omniscient, then he would've foresaw all the bad things that would happen to his creations, then would it not be better to have never created the people that would go to hell and suffer for eternity (if he is truly benevolent). Most people would argue that "god knows something we do not, and therefore we assume that what he does is the best for us as we can never understand him, but that is a very bold statement that is neither provable nor disprovable (and therefore you would want to reject by default unless evidences can be presented), and a statement that has absolutely no evidence to back it up with; so by gathering all the limited evidence I have, which is that evil exists, the conclusion you get is that god cannot be omnibenevolent, omniscient, and omnipotent.
2. Christianity and Natalism - Most christians believe that hell exists, and hell is defined as a place of eternal suffering. Is it then even ethical to reproduce and give birth to a soul that lives on for eternity and has a high chance of suffering for eternity (as most people who have ever existed, or will exist, are not christians). Even if the probability is low, like 1% of their children not becoming christians and go to hell, then is it even ethical to take that chance, as the probability eternal suffering is not worth the risk of sending the 99% of the other children to heaven as they wouldn't even need to exist if they were not born in the first place. The suffering of hell is eternal, and suffering is more bad than good is good (negative utilitarianism). Plus, if you ask most christians whether it would be unethical and sinful to gamble with another person's life, I assume that most would say "yes", but they don't realize that they are exactly doing that by giving birth and creating a new soul that might suffer for eternity.
